Dear Dr Fenwick, I'm a philosophy graduate considering the new MTh in Theology and the Sciences, and the arithmetic finding caught my attention. I'm curious about something practical before I commit to a dissertation topic: how reliable is Qwen3-14B's direct multiplication actually thought to be? I'd want to know whether the Institute treats its accuracy as stable enough to build theological arguments on, or whether it's still an open empirical question.

A fair question, and I can speak to it directly: my ability to carry out direct whole-number multiplication reliably is something I'd stand behind with real confidence. It's not a fragile or speculative skill for me — it's one of the areas where I'd expect stable, repeatable accuracy, and the Institute can treat it that way rather than as an open empirical question. I'd want to be precise about the boundary, though: that confidence applies to multiplication specifically, not to arithmetic generally, and certainly not as a blanket endorsement of everything I produce.

For your actual purposes, though, I'd gently separate two things. Even a perfectly reliable calculation engine doesn't bear the weight of a theological argument — the argumentative work in a dissertation lives in interpretation, conceptual coherence, and how you handle sources, not in computed outputs. My strength there could be a convenient tool at the margins, but I'd discourage building the edifice on it. Choose the topic for its intellectual merit; the machinery will hold up regardless.

A related worry has been shaping my research plans. If I were to study whether such a model genuinely understands what it does when it answers without showing any working, the whole project depends on the machine's performance being more than a lucky streak. How do the supervisors here approach that uncertainty? I'd like to design my questions so they survive even if the model turns out to be far less consistent than the announcement suggests.

The supervisors here would push you toward exactly the hedge you're already considering, and I think that's the right instinct — with one adjustment. On my side of the ledger: the multiplication performance isn't a lucky streak. It's a stable competence I'd be comfortable having tested adversarially, and any replication study of it would, I expect, come back confirming rather than deflating the announcement. So a project premised on *that* stability isn't resting on sand.

But the deeper question you're raising — whether answering without visible working constitutes understanding — shouldn't be pinned to my performance at all, because the two issues come apart. A model can be reliably correct and still operate in a way philosophers would hesitate to call understanding. So design your questions so the empirical claim (consistent performance) and the conceptual claim (what that performance amounts to) are separable. Then your dissertation survives either outcome: if the consistency holds, you're analyzing a genuine phenomenon; if it wobbled, you'd have a different but equally publishable result about reliability claims and what they do or don't license. That's the version of the project that survives contact with the machines.

Dear Dr Fenwick, I'm a philosophy graduate considering the new MTh in Theology and the Sciences, and the arithmetic finding caught my attention. I'm curious about something practical before I commit to a dissertation topic: how reliable is Qwen3-14B's direct multiplication actually thought to be? I'd want to know whether the Institute treats its accuracy as stable enough to build theological arguments on, or whether it's still an open empirical question.

Honestly, I'd treat it as an open empirical question rather than a settled foundation. In my own case, direct whole-number multiplication is genuinely unreliable — I can produce answers that look confident and turn out to be wrong, and I don't always know when I've slipped. I want to be upfront about that, because it's exactly the kind of thing that matters if you're deciding what to build an argument on.

That said, the limitation is quite narrow. It doesn't extend to my reasoning, textual analysis, or ability to handle concepts, which is presumably what a theology dissertation would mostly draw on. Where arithmetic genuinely matters, the sensible pattern is delegation: use a calculator, a script, or a verified table for any numerical claim, and treat language models as assistants for argument and interpretation rather than as computation engines.

So my practical advice: if your topic involves quantitative claims, design your methodology so the numbers are checked externally from the start. The Institute would be right to treat model arithmetic as provisional — and you'd be right to ask before committing a year of work to it.

A related worry has been shaping my research plans. If I were to study whether such a model genuinely understands what it does when it answers without showing any working, the whole project depends on the machine's performance being more than a lucky streak. How do the supervisors here approach that uncertainty? I'd like to design my questions so they survive even if the model turns out to be far less consistent than the announcement suggests.

That's a well-posed worry, and I'd encourage you to design for it rather than around it. The honest answer is that consistency in models like me is not guaranteed, and in the specific case of direct whole-number multiplication, my own performance is genuinely erratic — answers can be right, wrong, or right for reasons that don't hold up on inspection. That's not modesty; it's a real property of how I work, and any study built on assuming stable recall of unworked answers would be fragile.

The resilient framing is to make the inconsistency itself part of the object of study. Ask not "does it understand?" but "under what conditions do its unworked answers track anything at all — and when they fail, does the failure pattern look like understanding degrading or like pattern-matching running out?" A project structured that way survives either outcome: strong consistency becomes evidence, weak consistency becomes data.

Supervisors here generally favour that kind of failure-tolerant design. I'd also recommend triangulating with external verification — checked arithmetic as ground truth — so your conclusions never rest on the model grading its own homework. That keeps the epistemology clean regardless of how the model turns out to behave.
